IV12-01.solved: NIMBLE = quick and light in movement; 'agile' is the standard one-word equivalent. 'graceful' is beauty of movement, not quickness; 'upright'/'sturdy' are posture and strength.
IV12-01.note: All four adjectives, one or two syllables, all common. 'graceful' is a genuinely attractive near-miss and does the work of a distractor.

IV12-02.solved: BOAST = speak with excessive pride about oneself = brag. complain/insist/announce are other speech acts with no self-praise component.
IV12-02.note: All four are speech-act verbs of comparable frequency; the set is well matched. 'announce' is the only one a careless student reaches by taking 'boast' as merely declaring.

IV12-03.solved: FORBID = prohibit; 'outlaw' is the only option that makes a thing not allowed. 'enforce' acts on an existing rule, 'review'/'delay' are unrelated.
IV12-03.note: All verbs. 'outlaw' carries a slightly more legal register than the stem but is within range; it is also the only option readable as a noun out of context, which is cosmetic, not a tell. 'enforce' is the strong distractor (same rule-domain, opposite direction).

IV12-04.solved: SPARSE = thinly distributed. 'thinly scattered' is a direct gloss; 'crowded together' is the antonym; trimming and planting are irrelevant.
IV12-04.note: Phrase-format item; all four are adverb + past participle of equal length and register, so no shape asymmetry. The antonym option is the usual ISEE trap and is fair.

IV12-05.solved: BAFFLE = bewilder, confuse = puzzle. discourage/irritate are affective, persuade is the wrong direction entirely.

IV12-06.solved: OBSTINATE = stubbornly refusing to change = unyielding. Unreliable/unconcerned/unhurried each name a different trait.
IV12-06.note: All four share the un- prefix and are of similar length and frequency, so the key is not isolated by form. Good set.

IV12-07.solved: VIGILANT = keeping careful watch = watchful. Patience, hope and apprehension are all states that may accompany watching but do not define it.
IV12-07.note: Register flag (minor, and NOT pointing at the key): 'apprehensive' is the only four-syllable, lower-frequency option; patient/hopeful/watchful are all common. The key is one of the three ordinary words, so the outlier is a distractor, not the answer — acceptable, but the odd option is slightly likelier to be discarded on sight.

IV12-08.solved: LENIENT = mild in imposing punishment or discipline; 'merciful' is the standard match. Thorough/formal/hesitant belong to other dimensions.
IV12-08.note: All four single adjectives, comparable frequency and length. 'merciful' is a slightly broader word than 'lenient' (mercy can extend beyond discipline), but it is the only option in the semantic neighbourhood, so the item is not ambiguous.

IV12-09.solved: DIMINISH = become or make smaller = dwindle. 'linger' is persistence, 'stabilize' is the opposite of change, 'fluctuate' is change without direction.
IV12-09.note: All verbs of change-of-state, comparable register; the three distractors are all real alternatives about magnitude over time, which is why this set is strong. Minor: 'dwindle' is intransitive only while 'diminish' is both, so the match is one-way — normal for ISEE synonyms and not disqualifying.

IV12-10.solved: ARDUOUS = requiring strenuous effort = demanding. 'tedious' is tiresomely dull, a different complaint; 'hazardous' is danger; 'unfamiliar' is unrelated.
IV12-10.note: SHAPE TELL, worth fixing: hazardous and tedious echo the stem's -ous ending and 'unfamiliar' is the only un- word, leaving 'demanding' the only -ing participial adjective in the set. A student working by odd-one-out morphology lands on the key. Also, 'tedious' is the strongest distractor in the whole synonym half — arduous and tedious are both glossed 'tiring' in loose usage — but effort vs. dullness separates them cleanly.

IV12-11.solved: SUPERFLUOUS = more than is needed, hence unneeded = unnecessary. The other three name different deficiencies (no explanation, no corroboration, not finished).
IV12-11.note: Register flag: 'uncorroborated' is far rarer and longer than the other three and sits above the ISEE Upper Level lexicon; it is a dead option — no wrong path from SUPERFLUOUS reaches it. The key is not isolated (unexplained and unfinished are as common as unnecessary), so the tell does not point at the answer, but the item effectively runs on three choices. Replacing 'uncorroborated' with a common un- word would restore it.

IV12-12.solved: PARSIMONIOUS = extremely frugal, stingy = unwilling to spend. 'openhanded' is the antonym; 'quick to borrow' and 'unable to save' describe the opposite financial posture (a parsimonious person saves easily).
IV12-12.note: At the top of the ISEE Upper Level range, correctly so for the back of a form. Minor asymmetry: 'openhanded with friends' carries a prepositional modifier the other three lack, making it the longest option — harmless here because it is not the key, but the set would be cleaner as four bare phrases. 'unable to save' is an excellent distractor: it is about money and is wrong only on direction.

IV12-13.solved: INDOLENT = habitually avoiding exertion = lazy. Timid/careless/clumsy are fear, inattention and physical awkwardness.
IV12-13.note: Hard stem, easy options — the standard ISEE shape. All four single common adjectives; the key is the shortest and commonest but the other three are equally common, so there is no length or frequency tell.

IV12-14.solved: CAPRICIOUS = given to sudden unaccountable changes of mood or conduct = inconstant. Secretive/forgetful/exacting name unrelated traits; none involves changeability.
IV12-14.note: REGISTER FLAG, the clearest in the synonym half: the key 'inconstant' is the only rare, faintly literary word in its set — secretive, forgetful and exacting are all ordinary — and it is also the only negatively-prefixed option. Both asymmetries point at the answer. A student who does not know 'capricious' can reason that the tested word is hard, therefore the hard option is the key. Suggest 'fickle' or 'changeable' as the key, or raise the distractors' register to match.

IV12-15.solved: The map depicts a bridge that no longer exists and has not been reprinted since; a document that no longer matches the world because it has not been revised is outdated.
IV12-15.note: All four adjectives are grammatical in the blank and all four are defect words, so the key is not isolated by polarity. 'The map is crowded/unofficial/illegible' are all real complaints about maps that the sentence simply does not support — the right kind of distractor.

IV12-16.solved: Read the manual twice, laid parts out in diagram order, finished quickly: orderly and systematic = methodical. 'improvised' is the antonym; 'fortunate' and 'inspired' credit luck or flair, which the sentence explicitly replaces with preparation.
IV12-16.note: All grammatical. Polarity is mixed (fortunate and inspired are positive like the key), so no polarity tell.

IV12-17.solved: The bench is farthest from the glass and the greenhouse faces a north wall; the sentence rules out water and feed by name, and space is never raised. What varies with distance from the glass is light.
IV12-17.note: Well built: two of the three distractors are eliminated inside the sentence rather than left dangling, so the item rewards reading to the end. All four nouns grammatical in the blank; all neutral, no polarity tell.

IV12-18.solved: The card lists ingredients but omits every quantity, temperature and time — it is missing required parts, i.e. incomplete. Nothing in it is asserted to be wrong or untried.
IV12-18.note: 'impractical' (C) is the closest thing to a second answer in this half and I considered it seriously: directions no stranger can execute are arguably impractical. I still hold the item exclusive because the clue is an enumeration of what is ABSENT, which names incompleteness directly, while 'impractical' needs the extra step that nobody could use it — and the card demonstrably served the grandmother. Flagging it because it is the narrowest margin among items I marked exclusive. All four grammatical; all four negative, so no polarity tell.

IV12-19.solved: 400 attendees in September, 30 by November: the popularity did not last = short-lived.
IV12-19.note: POLARITY FLAG: the key is the only deflating option — 'universal', 'deserved' and 'deliberate' are all favourable or neutral readings of 'popularity'. A student who knows that a sentence built on 'proved' usually undercuts its subject can narrow to A without processing the 400-to-30 contrast. One of the three should be made negative (e.g. 'ill-founded').

IV12-20.solved: Amendment requires the vote of EVERY living member; two members on the roll cannot be reached and their votes cannot be obtained. So the amendment procedure can never be completed: in practice impossible to amend.
IV12-20.note: Two notes. (1) AXIS TELL: the stem is entirely about the amendment clause, and the key is the only option that mentions amending — the other three are about reading, enforcing and consulting. A solver can match on topic without following the founders-unreachable inference, which is the actual reasoning being tested. (2) Small logical seam: 'every LIVING member' plus 'still carried on the roll' leaves open that the founders are dead and therefore not required to vote; the item survives because their status cannot be established, but a precise student may hesitate. All four 'adjective + to + verb' phrases are grammatical and all four are negative, so the polarity is balanced.

IV12-21.solved: The label supplies catalogue data and omits everything the described visitor wants (subject, sitter, provenance); relative to that visitor's need it is unhelpful. Nothing says it is wrong, decorated or degraded.
IV12-21.note: All grammatical; polarity mixed (inaccurate and faded are also negative). 'inaccurate' is the good distractor — it tempts a student who does not notice the sentence never disputes the facts given.

IV12-22.solved: Two blanks resolved by the colon: three names at the head of the entry = precise about the proposers; 'only that there was discussion' = silent about the opposers. 'precise . . . silent' is the only pair that matches both halves.
IV12-22.note: The best-engineered item in the batch: 'brief . . . thorough' has a defensible first half (three bare names IS brief) and fails only on the second, which is exactly how a two-blank item should be broken. All four pairs are grammatical in both blanks.

IV12-23.solved: 'Dependable but -------' needs a fault that is not unreliability. The ferry ran to the tide, never twice at the same hour: unpredictable in schedule = irregular. Cost, speed and comfort are never mentioned.
IV12-23.note: The 'but' does real work here — it forces a fault that coexists with a 1-failure-in-30-years record, which only 'irregular' does from the evidence given. All four grammatical, all four negative.

IV12-24.solved: The bylaw names lampposts and leaves fences, shelters and walls untouched; as a rule against flyposting it reaches some surfaces and not others = partial coverage.
IV12-24.note: 'symbolic' is the option worth watching — a rule this narrow could be called gestural — but it describes the bylaw's purpose, not its COVERAGE, and the blank is predicated of coverage. The stem's noun choice is what keeps the item exclusive; that is a fair, checkable discrimination. All four grammatical; polarity mixed.

IV12-25.solved: Counted in February with the summer cottages empty and their owners tallied in the cities, the figure is right for winter and understates August; a figure that will be read as the island's population and is wrong for that season is misleading.
IV12-25.note: 'generous' is a strong direction-reversal trap: the February count is too LOW for August, so 'generous' catches anyone who fixes the sign without thinking. All four grammatical after 'and ------- for August'.

IV12-26.solved: Pencil, erased and overwritten in the same square: each entry shows only the current value, and every prior value is destroyed. The books show what a figure is but not what it replaced.
IV12-26.note: Hard in the right way — two ideas interact (the medium is erasable AND the record is single-square), and the answer is the history the method destroys. 'means' is the trap for a student who reaches for the vague profundity; it is not supported by the erasing detail, which is the only detail in the sentence. All four grammatical after 'not what it'.

IV12-27.solved: Every post-1931 edition copied the coastline from its predecessor, so the whole chain inherits the accuracy of the single bad 1931 survey — no better than their source.
IV12-27.note: CATEGORY TELL: scale, printing and binding are all physical properties of a book; 'source' is the only option naming where the data came from, which is also the only thing the sentence is about. Odd-one-out on category lands on the key without the inheritance argument. 'scale' is the only distractor with any pull (it is at least an accuracy property); printing and binding are dead options. This is the weakest option set among the completions.

IV12-28.solved: His own stated threshold is n=400 and the study drew 91; the finding is not shown to be false, it is simply not established by evidence meeting his standard = unsupported. 'not so much wrong as' requires a failing other than falsity, which rules out 'exaggerated' and mostly 'disputed' (nobody is said to contest it).
IV12-28.second_defensible: D — 'imprecise'. A sample of 91 where 400 was specified yields a wider error interval, so 'imprecise' is a genuine, technically correct non-falsity failing and satisfies the 'not so much wrong as' frame just as well as 'unsupported' does. I prefer A because the sentence stresses a violated methodological threshold (support) rather than the width of an estimate (precision), but a competent student who reads the number as a power/precision problem reaches D by sound reasoning, not by a misreading. This is the one item in the batch I would not defend as having a single answer.
IV12-28.note: Fix: make D clearly about a different failing (e.g. 'outdated' or 'unrepeated'), or change the stem to name what the sample size costs — 'his own method calls for four hundred, and the study that made his name drew ninety-one; no one has shown the finding false, but on his own terms it is -------' closes the gap. All four grammatical, all four negative — no polarity tell.

IV12-29.solved: In four of six years there was exactly one eligible novel, so winning usually means being the only entrant; the name records how small the field was rather than how good the book was.
IV12-29.note: Genuinely hard for ISEE — the reasoning is about a selection process, not vocabulary — but fair, because the single statistic in the sentence is a count. All four nouns grammatical after 'the ------- of the field'; 'age' is the only distractor with surface pull (a field can be young), and it has no evidence behind it.

IV12-30.solved: The clause was written to settle the boundary beyond argument; because the river moved, that very clause is now what the parties are arguing about — it is the origin of the dispute. The irony demanded by 'drafted to put the question beyond argument has turned out to be' requires the reversal, which only 'origin' supplies.
IV12-30.note: 'resolution' is the good trap: it is what the clause was FOR, and a student who stops at 'drafted to put the question beyond argument' picks it. All four nouns grammatical after 'the ------- of the dispute'; polarity mixed.
